items.title: $\sqrt2 + \sqrt3$ is irrational
items.prose: Prove that $\sqrt2 + \sqrt3$ is irrational. You may use that $\sqrt2$ is irrational, and that sums, differences, products and quotients of rationals are rational.
items.question: Put the proof in order. Move the three flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: $r > 0$, so $\sqrt2 = \tfrac{r^2 - 1}{2r}$, built from rationals by the four operations.
So $\sqrt2$ is rational, which is false. So $\sqrt2 + \sqrt3$ is irrational. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: You squared term by term. $(r - \sqrt2)^2 = r^2 - 2r\sqrt2 + 2$, with a cross term.
You supposed the claim. A contradiction proof supposes the opposite.

lines.text: The sum of two irrationals is irrational, so we are done.
lines.why: You used a false rule. $\sqrt2 + (-\sqrt2) = 0$ is rational.

feedback.correct: Right. Isolate one root, square, and solve for the other.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Isolate $\sqrt3$, square, then solve for $\sqrt2$.

byKey.d1: You used the term-by-term square. The cross term $-2r\sqrt2$ is what lets us solve for $\sqrt2$.
byKey.d2: You used the line supposing the claim. Suppose $\sqrt2 + \sqrt3$ is rational instead.
byKey.d3: You used the rule that irrational plus irrational is irrational. It is false: $\sqrt2 + (-\sqrt2) = 0$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the three flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Squaring $\sqrt3 = r - \sqrt2$ leaves $\sqrt2$ only in the cross term, so we can solve for it. $r > 0$ because $\sqrt2 + \sqrt3 > 0$, so dividing by $2r$ is safe. Then $\sqrt2$ is a quotient of rationals, a contradiction.

items.title: A threshold in epsilon
items.prose: Let $A = \{1 - \tfrac{1}{n^2} : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$, with $\sup A = 1$. Part two of the test asks for a term above $1 - \varepsilon$.
items.question: $1 - \tfrac{1}{n^2} > 1 - \varepsilon$ holds exactly when $n$ is greater than what? Give a formula in $\varepsilon$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Cancel the 1s, then solve $\tfrac{1}{n^2} < \varepsilon$ for $n$.

byKey.noroot: You solved for $n^2$, not $n$. $n^2 > \tfrac1\varepsilon$ gives $n > \tfrac{1}{\sqrt\varepsilon}$. Your bound works, but it is not exact.
byKey.root: You inverted the wrong way. Small $\varepsilon$ needs large $n$: $n > \tfrac{1}{\sqrt\varepsilon}$.

explain.text: $1 - \tfrac1{n^2} > 1 - \varepsilon$ is $\tfrac1{n^2} < \varepsilon$. Since $n > 0$, that is $n^2 > \tfrac1\varepsilon$, so $n > \tfrac{1}{\sqrt\varepsilon}$. Such an $n$ exists by the Archimedean property.

byKey.equal: You took $n = 100$. It gives exactly $1 - \tfrac{1}{10000} = 0.9999$, not above it.
byKey.noroot: You used $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$. The square on $n$ means $n > \tfrac{1}{\sqrt\varepsilon} = 100$.

explain.text: $\sqrt{0.0001} = 0.01$, so $n > 100$. At $n = 100$ the term equals 0.9999 exactly, so the smallest is 101.

items.title: Rationals below the root
items.prose: Let $T = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 2\}$, a set of rationals viewed inside $\mathbb{R}$.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: $\sup T = \sqrt2$ and $\inf T = -\sqrt2$, and neither is attained.

options.why: You left out negative rationals. $-1.4$ is in $T$, since $1.96 < 2$.

options.text: $T$ has no supremum, because $\sqrt2$ is not rational.
options.why: You looked for the supremum inside $\mathbb{Q}$. In $\mathbb{R}$, completeness gives $\sup T = \sqrt2$.

options.text: $\sup T = \sqrt2$, and it is the maximum of $T$.
options.why: You put $\sqrt2$ in $T$. It is irrational, and $(\sqrt2)^2 = 2$ is not less than 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the bounds in $\mathbb{R}$, then ask whether $T$ contains them.

explain.text: $\sqrt2$ bounds $T$ above, and density puts rationals of $T$ within any $\varepsilon$ below it. By symmetry $\inf T = -\sqrt2$. Neither is rational, so neither is in $T$.

items.title: A fraction near the root
items.prose: Find a fraction between $a = 1.414$ and $b = 1.4143$ by the recipe: the smallest whole $n > \tfrac{1}{b - a}$, then $m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1$.
items.question: Fill in $n$ and $m$.

byKey.r0c1: For $n$: $\tfrac{1}{0.0003} \approx 3333.33$, so the smallest whole number above it is 3334.

explain.text: $n = 3334$, so steps of $\tfrac{1}{3334} \approx 0.0003$ are narrower than the gap. $na = 4714.276$ gives $m = 4715$. Check: $1.414 < \tfrac{4715}{3334} \approx 1.4142172 < 1.4143$.

items.title: The 20th fraction
items.prose: Take the diagonal walk of the positive fractions, top row first, repeats skipped. $\tfrac15$ is 10th and $\tfrac51$ is 11th.
items.question: Which fraction is 20th? Give it as a fraction.

feedback.correct: Right. $\tfrac53$, the fifth fraction of diagonal 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Diagonal 7 fills places 12 to 17; diagonal 8 starts at 18.

byKey.before: You gave $\tfrac35$, the 19th. Count one more.
byKey.after: You gave $\tfrac71$, the 21st. Count one fewer.
byKey.repeat: You gave $\tfrac52$, the 20th cell if repeats are counted. Skip $\tfrac22$, $\tfrac24$, $\tfrac33$ and $\tfrac42$.

explain.text: Diagonal 7 holds all six of $\tfrac16, \dots, \tfrac61$: places 12 to 17. Diagonal 8 holds $\tfrac17, \tfrac35, \tfrac53, \tfrac71$, skipping $\tfrac26$, $\tfrac44$, $\tfrac62$. So place 20 is $\tfrac53$.

items.title: An irrational in every gap
items.prompt:
Prove that between any two real numbers there is an irrational number: for all $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$, some irrational $t$ has $a < t < b$.

You may use three facts. The rationals are dense (Whole numbers outrun everything). $\sqrt2$ is irrational (Gaps in the rationals). Sums and differences of rationals are rational. Give a reason for every line.
items.model:
**Claim.** For all real $a < b$ there is an irrational $t$ with $a < t < b$.

**Proof.** Let $a < b$ be real numbers.

1. Subtracting $\sqrt2$ from both sides keeps the order: $a - \sqrt2 < b - \sqrt2$.
2. By the density of $\mathbb{Q}$, applied to these two real numbers, there is a rational $r$ with $a - \sqrt2 < r < b - \sqrt2$.
3. Let $t = r + \sqrt2$. Adding $\sqrt2$ to each part of line 2 gives $a < t < b$.
4. Suppose, for a contradiction, that $t$ is rational. Then $\sqrt2 = t - r$ is a difference of two rationals, so it is rational.
5. That contradicts the irrationality of $\sqrt2$. So $t$ is irrational.

Since $a < b$ were arbitrary, every interval $(a, b)$ contains an irrational. $\blacksquare$

**Example.** For $a = 0.31$, $b = 0.32$: the rationals between $0.31 - \sqrt2 \approx -1.1042$ and $0.32 - \sqrt2 \approx -1.0942$ include $r = -1.1$, giving $t = \sqrt2 - 1.1 \approx 0.3142$.

**Another route.** Density gives a rational $r$ in $(a, b)$; then choose $n > \tfrac{\sqrt2}{b - r}$ and take $t = r + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{n}$. It lies in $(r, b)$, and it is irrational by the same argument as line 4.

rubric.text: Shifts the interval: applies density of $\mathbb{Q}$ to $(a - \sqrt2, b - \sqrt2)$. Or finds $r \in (a, b)$ and adds $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{n}$. Says why the ends stay in order.
Defines $t$ explicitly, such as $t = r + \sqrt2$, and shows $a < t < b$ from the inequalities for $r$.
Proves $t$ is irrational by contradiction: if $t$ were rational, $\sqrt2 = t - r$ would be rational.
Names the facts used: difference of rationals is rational, and $\sqrt2$ is irrational; uses no unproved claim such as irrational plus irrational is irrational.
Clear structure: lets $a < b$ be arbitrary and gives a reason on every line. States the conclusion for every interval.

items.title: Which set cannot be listed?
items.prose: Countable sets can be listed; the diagonal argument shows some sets cannot.
items.question: Which set is uncountable?

options.why: You chose the finite strings. List them by length, then in order: they are countable.
You chose a set the walk lists. Every subset of $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.

options.text: All pairs $(p, q)$ of whole numbers.
options.why: You chose the grid of pairs. The diagonal walk lists it, repeats and all.

feedback.correct: Right. Flip digit $k$ of the $k$th sequence to escape any list.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a set where a diagonal flip builds a new member.

explain.text: Given any list of 0-1 sequences, flip the $k$th entry of the $k$th sequence. The new sequence is in the set but differs from every listed one. Finite strings, rationals and pairs can all be listed.
